episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Wednesday, May sixth, twenty twenty-six.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Salesforce announced it will hire one thousand new graduates and interns to work on artificial intelligence projects, even as the company faces criticism for laying off roughly one thousand experienced employees earlier this year. CEO Marc Benioff made the announcement on X, calling the new recruits A.I. natives who will build products including Agentforce and Headless360. Fortune reported that the new Builder program places recent graduates in sales, product, and engineering roles specifically focused on A.I. initiatives. Benioff defines A.I. natives as people who use artificial intelligence daily and have an intuitive understanding of its potential. His announcement responded directly to Trump administration A.I. czar David Sacks, who cited data showing new college graduate hiring up five point six percent year-over-year and youth unemployment for degreed twenty to twenty-four year olds dropping from eight point nine percent to five point three percent. The company's hiring push comes against a backdrop of controversy. Critics labeled the strategy fire-and-rehire, arguing that Salesforce cut experienced workers to bring in cheaper recent graduates. The company laid off approximately one thousand employees in February 2025 and again in early 2026. Some industry observers defended the approach, arguing that companies have a responsibility to provide entry-level opportunities for new graduates entering the workforce. The debate reflects broader tensions in the technology sector about whether to hire experienced workers or recent graduates who grew up with the technology. Salesforce's hiring criteria specifically emphasize daily A.I. tool usage, a potential indicator for higher education institutions preparing students for careers in the field.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Working professionals in Arizona will soon be able to earn an artificial intelligence certificate without writing a single line of code. Scottsdale Community College announced its new Foundations of Applied A.I. Certificate of Completion, a nine-credit program launching this fall. Arizona Digital Free Press reported that the one-semester certificate requires no prerequisites and no coding background. The program targets managers, analysts, entrepreneurs, educators, and healthcare workers who need A.I. skills but not programming expertise. Students take three courses: A.I. Literacy and Everyday Applications, Applied A.I. Agents and Data Basics, and an A.I. Integration Project focused on real business applications in marketing, finance, operations, and customer experience. Nancy Dedakia, Computer Information Systems professor, said the college is not teaching students to build A.I. but to use it wisely, ethically, and effectively. Dr. Eric Leshinskie, SCC President, said the certificate represents the college's commitment to ensuring community members don't just watch that change happen, but help lead it.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Eight Trinity College seniors spent their final semester building artificial intelligence solutions for real community partners in Hartford, Connecticut. The students worked through the Applied A.I. Innovation Sandbox, a pilot program launched by the college's Elting Center for Innovation and Entrepreneurship. One five-student team partnered with Hartford city officials and Trinity security to review local CCTV footage, identifying vehicular and pedestrian safety issues around campus. Kwaku Agyapong and Ki Hwang developed healthcare A.I. applications with Connecticut Children's Medical Center. Two other students worked with Connecticut Invention Convention to create an A.I.-enabled curriculum tool that helps K-12 teachers access Google Classroom materials more efficiently. The program paired students with Cisco Systems, Google, and Microsoft as rapid-development team partners. Danny Briere, executive director of the Elting Center, said the students completed their real-world projects to client satisfaction and worked successfully alongside platform, vendor, and client partners as peers in scrum teams.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Alabama A. and M. University will become the first institution in Alabama to offer a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence when its inaugural cohort begins classes this fall. The historically Black university received approval from both its Board of Trustees and the Alabama Commission of Higher Education in 2025 for the 125-credit, four-year program. WHNT reported that the degree builds on computer science curriculum that has included an A.I. concentration since 2022. Students will study deep learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, and speech processing. Alabama A. and M. was recently selected as a regional lead institution for Amazon Web Services' Machine Learning University Program. Dr. ZT Deng, dean of the College of Engineering, Technology and Physical Sciences, said the university is responding to the changing demands of the market. Dr. John D. Jones, the university's provost, said students from other fields can take courses, gain exposure, and build the skills needed to work with A.I. tools.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Florida consumers may soon be shielded from paying higher electricity bills to subsidize large-scale A.I. data centers. Governor Ron DeSantis is expected to sign Senate Bill 484 at Florida Polytechnic University tomorrow, in what officials are calling the first legislation of its kind in the country. The law would prevent hyperscale data center utility expenses from being passed to Florida residents through rate increases. The legislation also establishes strict water use oversight for A.I. facilities, requiring public discussions about water impacts and consumptive use permits with monitoring caps. Data centers consume massive amounts of water for cooling their high-powered computing systems. Local governments would retain authority to approve and regulate data centers under the bill. If signed, the law takes effect July 1.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
